abstract: Abstract Background Enhancing immunogenicity and antigen-presentation efficiency is critical for tumor vaccine development. While yeast-surface glycoprotein side chains can improve antigen presentation, their ability to deliver tumor antigens remains limited. Methods The composite carbon nanopolymers (Asparagine-N-acetylglucosamine-Mannose derived carbon nanopolymers, ANM-NPs) mimicking yeast-surface glycans side chains were prepared using asparagine, N-acetylglucosamine and mannose as precursors via microwave-assisted synthesis method. Combined with whole-cell tumor antigen (T-Ag), the vaccine ANM-NPs@T-Ag was prepared. The expression levels of major histocompatibility complex-II, CD80, and CD86 were analyzed by flow cytometry to evaluate the enhancement of antigen presentation. The antitumor efficacy of ANM-NPs@T-Ag was assessed by H22-LUC and B16-F10-LUC tumor-bearing models. Results ANM-NPs have an average particle size of approximately 21.69 nm and exhibit good stability. Compared with traditional aluminum adjuvants, ANM-NPs demonstrate superior efficacy in promoting antigen presentation and immune activation. ANM-NPs effectively stimulated innate immunity, facilitated immune cell infiltration, and enhanced adaptive immune responses. The vaccine ANM-NPs@T-Ag targeted dendritic cells via mannose receptors, activating the lectin pathway, improving complement opsonization, and enhancing antigen presentation. ANM-NPs@T-Ag stimulated cellular/humoral immunity, increased tumor-specific IgG, and inhibited tumor growth. ANM-NPs@T-Ag also enhanced the antitumor effect of α-PD-1 (programmed cell death protein-1). Conclusion These findings demonstrate that ANM-NPs can serve as a potential vaccine adjuvant, and ANM-NPs@T-Ag represents a promising tumor vaccine candidate.Cite Now

WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC
Current cancer treatments increasingly depend on immunotherapies, which aim to stimulate the immune system to recognize and eliminate tumor cells. However, their effectiveness is often limited by poor antigen presentation and the low immunogenicity of conventional protein antigens, leading to specific immune responses in just 11–50% of patients. Enhancing immunogenicity and improving antigen-presentation efficiency are crucial in tumor vaccine development. Yeast-surface-glycoprotein side chains can promote antigen presentation, yet have drawbacks in carrying tumor antigens.
WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS
To improve tumor vaccine efficacy, we developed a novel biomimetic vaccine adjuvantAsparagine-N-acetylglucosamine-Mannose derived carbon nanopolymers (ANM-NPs). ANM-NPs are structurally designed to mimic the glycan side chains of yeast, thereby enhancing antigen presentation and potentiating immune activation. Compared with conventional aluminum adjuvants, ANM-NPs more effectively promote antigen presentation, activate innate and adaptive immunity via targeting mannose receptors and complement receptors. And ANM-NPs combined with tumor antigens (ANM-NPs@tumor antigen (T-Ag)) also significantly boost immune cell infiltration and suppress tumor growth.
HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY
This study introduces an innovative strategy to enhance antigen presentation and immune activation in cancer immunotherapy. ANM-NPs can be developed as a novel vaccine adjuvant, and ANM-NPs@T-Ag may be a promising tumor vaccine candidate.
Introduction
Tumor immunotherapy primarily aims to activate or enhance the body’s immune system, maintaining its effectiveness, specificity, and memory to achieve the goal of killing tumor cells.
1
However, in tumor cells, only about 1% of tumor-specific antigens are presented to the immune system.
2
Additionally, due to the low immunogenicity of traditional protein antigens, only a small percentage of patients (11–50%) are able to produce a specific immune response.
3
Developing effective tumor vaccine adjuvants might be an effective strategy for enhancing the efficiency of tumor antigen presentation and increasing the success rate of tumor vaccine development.
Currently, tumor vaccine adjuvants mainly include lipids, polymers, inorganic materials, and biomimetic nano-adjuvants.
4
However, these adjuvants face multiple challenges in practical applications, including issues with safety, antigen presentation efficacy, and application limitations. For example, aluminum adjuvants fail to activate Th1/CD8
+
T-cell responses and have narrow antigen compatibility.
5
Additionally, many adjuvants, such as aluminum adjuvants, lose effectiveness after freezing and thawing, while the immunostimulant saponin QS21 is limited by low yield, high cost, and poor stability.
6
Moreover, the unclear mechanisms of some adjuvants hinder their development and limit the combined use of different adjuvants.
7
Based on the above background, this study is dedicated to researching new antitumor vaccine adjuvants.
Tumor immunity involves complex interactions between the innate and adaptive immune systems, where pathogen-associated molecular patterns promote sustained adaptive immunity by enhancing antigen presentation, which is essential for activating immune responses in tumor vaccines.
8
The mannose receptor, a type of pattern recognition receptor in the C-type lectin receptor family, recognizes carbohydrates on the surface of pathogenic microorganisms in the presence of Ca²
+
and is mainly expressed on immune cells such as macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs).
9
DCs use the mannose receptor to absorb antigens from the environment via micropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and clathrin-mediated endocytosis. Additionally, carbohydrates on pathogenic microorganisms can activate the lectin pathway, promoting complement opsonization and enhancing antigen presentation.
10
Complement receptors on phagocytes interact with complement proteins such as C3b/iC3b deposited on pathogens, activating phagocytosis.
11
Studies have shown that glycan side chains on yeast surface glycoproteins can promote antigen presentation through the above pathways. However, the limited antigen binding ability and tumor targeting properties restrict their direct application.
Due to advantages such as ease of synthesis, chemical stability, and biocompatibility, carbon nanopolymers are receiving increased attention in the biomedical field.
12
Carbon nanopolymers are typically nanomaterials with a polymer-carbon hybrid structure prepared by bottom-up synthesis methods. The bottom-up approach focuses on the cross-linking reactions of molecules or polymers rich in amino, hydroxyl, or other active groups, wherein polymerization and carbonization play crucial roles in particle formation. Commonly used preparation methods include hydrothermal, solvothermal, microwave-assisted, and various other techniques. The diversity of carbon sources and synthesis methods endows carbon nanopolymers with structural and property versatility.
13
The formation of carbon nanopolymers primarily involves four processes: dehydration, polymerization, carbonization, and surface passivation.
14
The typical characteristic of carbon nanopolymers is a core-shell structure, consisting of an inner hydrophobic core made of partially carbonized precursors containing graphite-like microcrystals, and an outer hydrophilic shell enveloping the core, which retains a large number of uncarbonized polymer chains and abundant functional groups (eg, -OH, -COOH, -NH₂).
15
This unique core-shell structure mainly contains elements such as C, N, and O, granting them good water dispersibility, low toxicity, and excellent biocompatibility. In addition, the preparation of carbon nanopolymers can also enhance the biological activity of the precursor components.
16
When appropriately sized carbon nanopolymers are designed as tumor vaccine adjuvants, they can bind with antigens and enable targeted, controlled antigen release.
17
Based on the above-mentioned background, the carbon nanopolymers mimicking the glycan components of yeast surface glycoproteins may enhance the antigen presentation.
18
In the glycan side chains, mannose serves as the primary component of mannan side chains, asparagine acts as the critical linkage between glycans and proteins, and N-acetylglucosamine acts as the critical linkage between mannose and asparagine. Since mannan chains are crucial components for the immune activation, mannose was selected as the main carbon source precursor of the carbon nanopolymers. The amino group of asparagine readily undergoes the Maillard reaction with the aldehyde group of reducing sugars, facilitating the formation of the “carbon core” of the carbon nanopolymers. N-acetylglucosamine, a key component of chitin, was incorporated into the carbon nanopolymers system to improve structural stability while simultaneously providing immunostimulatory properties. Thus, theANM-NPs mimicking yeast surface glycans side chains were prepared from asparagine (Asn), N-acetylglucosamine (NAG), and mannose (Man) precursors via microwave-assisted synthesis. After incubating ANM-NPs with the whole-tumor antigen (T-Ag) to prepare a tumor vaccine (ANM-NPs@T-Ag), it was found that the incubated antigen could bind to the mannose receptor and induce C3b/iC3b enrichment on the antigen surface, enhancing presentation capabilities and recruitment of immune cells, leading to a significant tumor growth inhibition effect (
figure 1
). Furthermore, this study found that combining ANM-NPs@T-Ag with immune checkpoint inhibitors had synergistic effects.

D-luciferin potassium (150 µg/g, meilunstar, 115144-35-9) was injected intraperitoneally into the mice, and the mice were anesthetized when the peak fluorescein uptake was reached 10 min after the injection, and then imaged, and the bioluminescent intensity was calculated using Living Image software.
Incubation of mouse serum with ANM-NPs@T-Ag
Fresh non-heat-inactivated mouse serum was incubated separately with ovalbumin (OVA) and ANM-NPs@OVA at room temperature for 2 hours.
ELISA assay
The experiment was conducted according to the instructions provided in the ELISA kit manual. Briefly, samples and standards were added to the wells of the ELISA plate, followed by the addition of the detection antibody. The plate was then incubated at the specified temperature and time outlined in the manual. After washing the wells to remove unbound substances, a substrate solution was added to each well. The enzyme-substrate reaction was stopped after the recommended time, and the absorbance was measured at the appropriate wavelength using a microplate reader. Data were analyzed according to the ELISA kit protocol to quantify the analyte concentrations.
In-gel digestion
Load the protein samples onto the gel and perform electrophoresis. Once the separation is complete, remove the target bands from the sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) gel under protective conditions and collect the gel pieces. Destain the gel by incubating it in 50 mM NH
4
HCO
3
/50% acetonitrile until the gel becomes transparent, then dehydrate with acetonitrile until the gel pieces turn white. Dry the gel pieces at 37°C. Reduce and alkylate the proteins by incubating the gel pieces with 10 mM DTT in 25 mM NH
4
HCO
3
at 56°C for 50 min, followed by alkylation with iodoacetamide (IAA) at room temperature in the dark for 40 min. After alkylation, further, destain and dehydrate the gel pieces, then dry them completely. Prepare a trypsin solution (10 ng/µL in 25 mM NH
4
HCO
3
) and incubate with the gel pieces at room temperature for 1 min, then at 4°C for 5 min. Perform digestion overnight at 37°C with shaking. After digestion, collect the supernatant by centrifuging, then extract peptides sequentially with 1% formic acid in 2% acetonitrile, 50% acetonitrile, and 1% formic acid in acetonitrile. Combine the extracts, dry the final solution, and prepare it for mass spectrometry analysis.
Proteomics sample preparation and analysis
In this experiment, mouse serum proteins are purified using in-gel digestion, followed by proteomics analysis through liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC/MS). Initially, mouse serum samples undergo in-gel digestion to separate proteins from the gel matrix. The gel residues are then removed by centrifugation or filtration to obtain purified protein samples. These purified proteins are subsequently subjected to separation using a liquid chromatography system and analyzed by mass spectrometry to generate protein mass spectrometry data. Finally, specialized data analysis software is employed for protein identification, providing proteomics information for mouse serum, which is further analyzed using R V.4.3.1.
Assessment of OVA/ANM-NPs formation ability
Using a Jasco J715 spectrometer, the measurement data were recorded at a constant temperature of 25°C, and the spectral values in the wavelength range of 190–250 nm were determined. The results of the obtained data will be used to predict the proportion of various secondary structures in the protein online through DichroWeb.
Cell proliferation assay
Cell proliferation ability was assessed by Cell Counting Kit-8 (APExBIO, K1018). According to the manufacturer’s instructions, after T-Ag inoculation at 0, 24, 48, and 72 hours, 10 µL of Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) solution was added to each well, and incubated at 37°C for 2 hours. The absorbance of each well was measured at a wavelength of 450 nm using a microplate reader (Thermo Fisher).
Interaction between ANM-NPs@OVA and iC3b (immunoprecipitation, co-IP)
Beads preparation: wash 60 µL magnetic beads in 1 mL washing buffer (10% radio immunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) Lysis buffer in PBS) using a magnetic stand, and repeat. Antibody incubation: add diluted antibody to beads, incubate 2 hours at room temperature with rotation, then wash three times. Protein preparation: measure protein concentration with bicinchoninic acid assay (BCA) assay. Perform serial dilutions of bovine serum albumin (BSA) standard, add samples and BCA working solution, incubate at 37°C for 30 min, and measure absorbance. Binding: add protein samples to antibody-bound beads, incubate overnight at 4°C. Washing: wash beads several times with buffer, discard supernatant. Elution: add 1×loading buffer, heat at 95°C for 10 min, and recover supernatant. Then the supernatant was detected by western blot.
Western blot
Western blot was performed as previously described.
19
The proteins were separated through SDS polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred to polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. After being blocked in 5% skim milk for 2 hours at room temperature, the membranes were incubated with primary antibodies (C3b, RRID:AB_1073822) at 4°C overnight and secondary antibodies at room temperature for 2 hours.
Isolation and activation of BMDCs
To collect BMDCs, 7-week-old C57BL/6 mice were euthanized, sterilized by immersion in 75% ethanol, and the tibiae and femurs were removed and the bones were rinsed with PBS to obtain bone marrow cells. After centrifugation and collection, the bone marrow cells were cultured in Roswell Park Memorial Institute 1640 medium (10% fetal bovine serum) containing 20 ng/mL granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF, Abclonal, RP01206) and 10 ng/mL interleukin (IL)-4 (Abclonal, RP01161). On day 3, the supernatant is gently removed and the same fresh medium is added. On day 7, BMDCs were collected and spread evenly in 6-well plates at a density of 1×10
6
cells. The experimental group was treated with 1×10
6
ANM-NPs@T-Ag and 5% non-heat-inactivated serum from mice, while the control group consisted of wells without ANM-NPs@T-Ag. After 48 hours of treatment, BMDCs were collected and cells were stained with antibodies CD80 (PTMa, PTM-5247), CD86 (PTMa, PTM-5570) and MHC-II (Invitrogen, 14-5321-82), respectively. The secondary antibody CoraLite 488-conjugated Goat Anti-Mouse IgG (H+L) (Proteintech, SA00013-1) was used, and analyzed using flow cytometry.
Messenger RNA sequencing
Treat mouse primary DCs with ANM-NPs@T-Ag and heat-inactivated mouse serum. Extract total RNA from both untreated and treated cells using TRIzol. Measure RNA quantity and quality with NanoDrop (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Construct DNA libraries using the Illumina Nextera XT DNA library preparation kit (Illumina), which is based on the KAPA RNA-Seq library preparation method and employs oligo (dT) magnetic beads for RNA enrichment. Assess library quality with an Agilent 4200 (Agilent). Purify library fragments to select for complementary DNA fragments of approximately 200 bp using the AMPure XP system (Beckman Coulter). Verify the library by electrophoresis, pool the libraries, and sequence on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 (150 bp, paired-end; Illumina). RNA sequencing is performed by BGI Biotechnology. Differential analysis is conducted using the DESeq R package.
BMDCs induction and competitive inhibition study
Preincubate cells with different concentrations of αCD206 (BioLegend), αCD209 (BioLegend), or isotype control antibodies (Thermo Fisher) at 37°C for 20 min. Then, add ANM-NPs@T-Ag to the cell culture medium and incubate at 37°C for 48 hours. After incubation, wash the cells two times with cell culture medium. Finally, assess the expression of MHC-II on DC surfaces using flow cytometry to evaluate competitive inhibition.
DCs T-cell co-cultures
CD8
+
T cells were isolated and purified from the spleen of 7-week-old C57BL/6 mice using the CD8
+
T Cell Isolation Kit (BioLegend, 480008). After DCs maturation, DCs and T cells were co-cultured at a 1:10 ratio at 10
6
T cells/mL in RPMI-1640 supplemented with 10% serum. 20 ng/mL GM-CSF (Abclonal, RP01206) and 10 ng/mL IL4 (Abclonal, RP01161) were added to some cultures.
T-cell proliferation assay
Carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE)-labeled T cells (0.3 µM CFSE) were cultured alone or in the presence of induced DCs in RPMI-1640 with l-glutamine supplemented with 10% serum in 6-well plates. Flow cytometry was performed to assess proliferation of T cells.
Flow cytometry analysis
Tumor or spleen tissues from mice in each group were collected, the tumors were cut into small pieces with scissors, and digested with 1 mg/mL collagenase IV (Solarbio, C8160) at 37°C for 1 hour. The digested tissues were filtered through a 100 µm cell filter and collected to obtain a single-cell suspension. Cells were fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 min, followed by staining with a series of fluorophore-coupled antibodies for 30 min at 4°C in the dark. The following antibodies were used: anti-mouse CD45 APC (Invitrogen, 17-0451-83), anti-mouse CD3 FITC (BioLegend, 100204), anti-mouse CD4 PE (Invitrogen, 12-0441-83), anti-mouse CD8 PE (sungene, M1008309D), anti-mouse CD8a 605 (BioLegend, 100743), anti-mouse CD62L APC (Invitrogen, 17–0621- 82), anti-Hu/Mo CD44 PE (Invitrogen, 12-0441-82). All samples were collected on a flow cytometer (BD LSRFortessa) and data were analyzed by FlowJo software.
Statistical analysis
All results were generated without any data screening/selection procedures. Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism software V.8 (La Jolla, California, USA) and results were presented as mean±SD. Comparisons between two groups were assessed by t-test or one-way analysis of variance and Dunnett’s test (for multiple comparisons). The statistically significant values were set as *p<0.05 and **p<0.01.

ANM-NPs exhibit strong antigen-binding capability and can activate antitumor immunity
To stimulate innate immune responses and further enhance antigen presentation, we mimicked the glycan structure of yeast surface glycoproteins to prepare biomimetic carbon nanopolymers as tumor vaccine adjuvants. Using microwave heating method, we separately synthesized carbon nanopolymers of Man-NPs, Asn-NPs, and NAG-NPs, as well as the composite carbon polymers (ANM-NPs) using the above three monomers (
figure 2A
). The synthesized different carbon nanopolymers all had a particle size distribution around 20 nm, with an average particle size of 21.69 nm for ANM-NPs, which favors lymph node targeting (
figure 2B,C
, and
online supplemental figure S1A
).
20
After freeze-drying and redispersing in an aqueous solution, the nanoparticle size of the carbon nanopolymers remained stable for up to 48 hours (
figure 2D
). Ultraviolet-visible absorption and emission spectra indicated strong absorption in the 200–250 nm range, with a redshift compared with each raw material (
figure 2E
and
online supplemental figure S1B
). Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy showed that the O-H, N-H, C=O, and C-O bond vibrations of the synthesized carbon nanopolymers differed from those of the monosaccharide raw materials, likely due to polymerization (
figure 2F
and
online supplemental figure S1C
). Man-NPs and Asn-NPs exhibited negative charges, whereas NAG-NPs and ANM-NPs were positively charged, with a Zeta potential of 19.2 mV for ANM-NPs (
figure 2G
). The experiment shows that the synthesized carbon nanopolymers are stable. XPS analysis determined the composition of ANM-NPs as C 54.44%, N 6.18%, and O 39.39%. The lower nitrogen content compared with other carbon nanopolymers suggests a higher incorporation of mannose, which is nitrogen-free (
online supplemental figure S1D
). This resulting structure more closely mimics the glycosylation pattern found on yeast surface proteins, enhancing its biomimetic properties.
21

To verify the antitumor effects of the above carbon nanopolymers, we established the subcutaneous tumor-bearing mice model using B16-F10-LUC cells and injected different carbon nanopolymers into the tumor tissues. Results showed that ANM-NPs had the best inhibition effects on tumor growth than the single-component carbon nanopolymers (eg, Man-NPs and Asn-NPs) and the mixture of monomers (
figure 2H,I
). Additionally, ANM-NPs achieved a tumor inhibition rate of up to 47.9%, higher than other carbon nanopolymers and the mixture of monomers. ELISA results showed that ANM-NPs significantly increased IgG levels in mice serum, with IgG levels rising 3.13-fold, which is better compared with the single-component carbon nanopolymers, indicating a notable enhancement in humoral immune activation by ANM-NPs (
figure 2J
). Flow cytometry analysis showed that ANM-NPs had the most prominent enrichment effect on CD45
+
, CD3
+
, and CD8
+

figure 2K
and
online supplemental figure S1E
). LC/MS analysis of protein content in mice serum indicated a significant increase in antibody-related and complement-related proteins in the ANM-NPs group (
figure 2L
). These findings suggest that ANM-NPs, compared with single-component carbon nanopolymers, are the optimal carbon nanopolymers for suppressing tumor growth while promoting immune cell enrichment and activating humoral immunity.
To evaluate the antigen-binding ability of ANM-NPs, OVA was used as a model antigen. At 4°C, 10 mg of OVA was mixed with 1 mg of each carbon nanopolymers for 1 hour to form complexes. Circular dichroism analysis showed that 10% ANM-NPs@OVA, 10% Man-NPs@OVA, and 10% NAG-NPs@OVA retained OVA’s secondary structure,
22
suggesting that ANM-NPs did not disrupt the antigen’s secondary structure (
online supplemental figure S2A
). Based on the comparison of carbon nanopolymers in terms of complex stability and immune response activation, ANM-NPs were selected for further study.
ANM-NPs@T-Ag promote dendritic cells maturation and T cells activation
Whole-cell tumor antigens can overcome the limitations of single tumor antigen and activate CD8
+
T cells and CD4
+
T cells. To enhance the antitumor activity of ANM-NPs, we developed a novel tumor vaccine by combining ANM-NPs with whole-cell tumor antigens (ANM-NPs@T-Ag) and conducted the subsequent evaluations. The whole-cell tumor antigens were prepared from tumor cell lysates subjected to repeated freeze-thaw cycles in liquid nitrogen. CCK8 assay was used to confirm the absence of live tumor cells in the antigen preparation (
online supplemental figure S2B
). Injection of the tumor antigen into C57BL/6N mice also showed no tumorigenicity (
online supplemental figure S2C,D
).
We first compared the effects of ANM-NPs loaded with whole-cell tumor antigens (T-Ag (OVA)) on DCs and T cells to those of aluminum adjuvant (alum) loaded, which is the “gold standard” for adjuvant development.
23
DCs activation or “maturation” regulation is crucial in driving the antitumor immunity cycle, as DCs are essential in initiating T-cell responses and maintaining T-cell functionality.
24
To enhance ANM-NPs’ antitumor activity and assess the antitumor efficacy of the tumor vaccine, we combined T-Ag (OVA) with ANM-NPs by rotating the mixture at 4°C for 1 hour, obtaining ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) (
figure 3A
). In order to test the specificity of antigen presentation, we used the B16-F10-OVA cells to prepare whole-cell tumor antigens. In the B16-F10-OVA subcutaneous tumor model, ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) intratumorally treatment significantly suppressed tumor growth (
figure 3B
). ELISA results showed that animals treated with ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) had anti-OVA IgG titers higher than those in other treatment groups (
figure 3C
), indicating a marked activation of humoral immunity induced by ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA). Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and IFN-γ promote nitric oxide production and cell death via the JAK/STAT1/IRF1 axis. IFN-γ regulates immune gene expression, enhances macrophage and antitumor activity, and promotes T-cell activation and Th1/Th2 differentiation.
25
Further analysis showed that ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) incubated in non-heat-inactivated mouse serum significantly increased TNF-α levels in DC supernatants. When these DCs were co-cultured with CD8
+
T cells, the IFN-γ level in the supernatant also increased (
figure 3D
). Analysis of MHC-II, CD80, and CD86 expression on DCs surfaces showed that ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) incubated in non-heat-inactivated mouse serum markedly enhanced DCs antigen presentation (
figure 3E,F
). To directly demonstrate antigen-specific T-cell activation, we evaluated the response of pre-existing effector tumor antigen-specific T cells (ETASTs) using the ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA)-based assay. In this system, antigen-presenting cells (APCs) phagocytose the nanoparticles, process the encapsulated whole tumor antigens, and present them via MHC molecules.
26
The subsequent T-cell activation, primarily dependent on T cell antigen receptor signaling (Signal 1) for pre-committed ETASTs, was quantified by measuring IFN-γ production.
27 28
Our results confirm the robust induction of antigen-specific T-cell immunity following ANM-NPs@T-Ag vaccination treatment (
figure 3G
). Lastly, using CFSE-labeled CD8
+
T cells, we observed that ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) incubated DCs in non-heat-inactivated mouse serum more effectively promoted CD8
+
T-cell proliferation (
figure 3H
). In the mouse tumor model, ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) increased anti-OVA IgG levels in vivo, enhanced DCs antigen presentation capacity and TNF-α secretion, and boosted CD8
+
T-cell proliferation and IFN-γ secretion more effectively than aluminum adjuvant.

ANM-NPs@T-Ag has good safety and biocompatibility
To assess the safety of ANM-NPs@T-Ag, in which T-Ag were prepared with B16-F10-LUC cells, we incubated it with LO2, RAW264.7, and B16-F10-LUC cells at a 1:1 antigen-to-cell ratio, respectively, and used the CCK8 assay to evaluate its cytotoxicity. Results showed no significant effect on cell viability of the above cell types (
online supplemental figure S3A
). C57BL/6 mice were subcutaneously injected with either 200 µL of ANM-NPs@T-Ag (ANM-NPs@T-Ag group) or PBS (Con group) on days 1, 4, and 9. After 21 days, heart, liver, spleen, lung, and kidney tissues were collected, weighed, and analyzed using H&E staining. No notable tissue damage was observed in all the organs (
online supplemental figure S3B–D
). IgE levels and body temperature are common indicators of hypersensitivity. ELISA results showed a 1.71-fold increase in serum IgE levels in the ANM-NPs@T-Ag group (
online supplemental figure S3E
). Importantly, the absence of significant elevation in liver enzymes alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate transaminase (AST)) confirms that the treatment does not induce hepatotoxicity, indicating the good biocompatibility of ANM-NPs@T-Ag (
online supplemental figure S3E
).
29
During the treatment, a slight increase of approximately 1°C in body temperature was observed (
online supplemental figure S3F
). In conclusion, ANM-NPs@T-Ag effectively activates immune responses with no significant impact on cell viability. Although a mild increase in IgE levels and body temperature was noted in the mice, there was no evident hypersensitivity reaction, and no damage to major organs was observed, demonstrating good biocompatibility of ANM-NPs@T-Ag.
ANM-NPs@T-Ag activate the complement pathway and dendritic cells immune response
Complement proteins in serum can interact with complement receptors on phagocytes, further promoting phagocytic activity.
11
Primarily derived from the liver and widely distributed in serum, complement proteins can be analyzed using proteomics to determine their levels.
30
We conducted a proteomic analysis of serum from both the control group and the ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) group. LC/MS results showed significant expression differences, with complement-related and antibody-related genes markedly upregulated in the treatment group (
figure 4A
and
online supplemental figure S4A
). Gene Ontology analysis further indicated significant enrichment of biological processes related to acute inflammatory response and complement activation (
figure 4B
), and the gene-pathway interaction network demonstrated the interactions among various proteins involved in acute inflammatory response and the complement system (
figure 4C
). ELISA analysis revealed a significant increase in serum C3b protein levels in the ANM-NPs@T-Ag (OVA) group (
figure 4D
), with C3b serving as a central component in the complement cascade. To assess the binding ability of ANM-NPs@OVA to the C3b protein in serum, we employed co-immunoprecipitation to detect the amount of C3b associated with OVA. Fresh, non-heat-inactivated mouse serum was incubated with either OVA or ANM-NPs@OVA at room temperature for 2 hours. An antibody specific for OVA was used to immunoprecipitate the complexes, which were then separated by SDS-PAGE, and western blot analysis was performed using an antibody against C3b. High levels of C3b protein were detected in the ANM-NPs@OVA immunoprecipitate but were lower in control immunoprecipitates, with no interaction observed in non-specific IgG (
figure 4E
). We extracted DCs induced by non-heat-inactivated serum and ANM-NPs@T-Ag using a DC extraction kit and conducted bulk-RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) (
figure 4F
). Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes analyses showed that ANM-NPs@T-Ag significantly activated DCs innate immune responses, MHC-I molecule expression, and pathways related to C-type lectin receptors (
figure 4G
and
online supplemental figure S4B–D
). BMDCs were pretreated with antibodies against DCs-expressed mannose internalization receptors CD206 and CD209
31
and then treated with ANM-NPs@T-Ag. Results showed that increasing concentrations of αCD206 or αCD209 reduced BMDCs MHC-II fluorescence signals (
figure 4H
). BMDCs were treated with different concentrations of ANM-NPs and T-Ag complexes, and MHC-II-associated fluorescence intensity was measured using flow cytometry. As expected, higher ANM-NPs concentrations increased BMDCs MHC-II fluorescence signals (
figure 4I
). MBL was removed from extracted serum using mannose-binding lectin magnetic beads to produce MBL
−/−
serum, which was then added to the induced DCs system.
32
Flow cytometry analysis showed that the addition of normal non-heat-inactivated mouse serum activated DCs antigen presentation of ANM-NPs@T-Ag more effectively than MBL
−/−
non-heat-inactivated mouse serum (
figure 4J,K
). To investigate whether ANM-NPs@T-Ag acts on the mannose receptor (CD206), we knocked down CD206 in DC2.4 cells using siRNA, and the results demonstrated that reduced CD206 expression led to impaired antigen presentation capacity (
online supplemental figure S4E
). These results indicate that ANM-NPs@T-Ag can target BMDCs mannose-binding C-type lectins CD206 and CD209, as well as complement receptors, thereby enhancing antigen presentation.

Discussion
Tumor vaccines still face several challenges in cancer immunotherapy, such as the immunosuppressive effects of the tumor microenvironment, downregulation of MHC-I on cancer cells, and low activation efficiency of APCs. Enhancing immunogenicity and improving antigen presentation efficiency are key objectives in the development of tumor vaccines. Currently, vaccine adjuvants primarily include lipids, polymers, inorganic materials, and biomimetic nano-adjuvants. Compared with other vaccine adjuvants, carbon nanopolymers offer advantages such as ease of preparation, high safety, and good chemical inertness.
12
In this study, we designed and prepared carbon nanopolymers (ANM-NPs) as potential antigen adjuvants based on the glycan structures of yeast surface glycoproteins. Furthermore, we developed ANM-NPs@T-Ag, a novel vaccine platform where ANM-NPs function dually as delivery carriers and immunoadjuvants for the whole-tumor antigens.
The formation of carbon nanopolymers typically involves processes such as polymerization, cross-linking, dehydration, and carbonization.
40
Multiple substances serve as precursors, facilitating the formation of the core structure of carbon nanopolymers, thereby enhancing polymerization, cross-linking, and carbonization. The composite carbon nanopolymers (ANM-NPs) mimicking yeast-surface glycans side chains were prepared using Man, Asn, and NAG as precursors via microwave-assisted synthesis method. Microwave methods increase effective molecular collisions, leading to dehydration reactions between functional groups, which result in longer polymer chains and a certain degree of cross-linking.
41
The principle of the microwave reaction method is based on a dielectric heating mechanism, whereby polar molecules (eg, water, monomers) or ions in the reaction system undergo high-frequency oscillation and friction under the influence of the microwave electromagnetic field, thus instantaneously and efficiently converting microwave energy into molecular internal energy to achieve rapid and uniform volumetric heating of the reaction system. This method can extremely efficiently drive the key processes of polymerization, cross-linking, and carbonization critical to the synthesis of carbon nanopolymers, significantly reducing the reaction time from several hours to just a few minutes.
42
The characterization results showed that ANM-NPs have an average particle size of about 20 nm and exhibit good stability. The function results indicated that ANM-NPs effectively enhanced antigen presentation efficiency through interactions with mannose receptors and complement-mediated opsonization, further promoting the infiltration of immune cells.
The tumor immunity cycle consists of several key stages: release of cancer cell antigens (through cancer cell death); presentation of tumor antigens (by specialized APCs); activation and initiation of immune responses (by APCs and T cells); transport of T cells to the tumor site; infiltration of T cells into the tumor and stroma; and recognition and killing of cancer cells by T cells.
33 43
Exogenous protein antigens are taken up by APCs (such as DCs) through processes like phagocytosis, endocytosis, or direct acquisition from the surface of live cells. The engulfed exogenous protein antigens enter phagosomes, which can lead to two pathways for entering the cytoplasm: (1) rupture of the phagosome, allowing antigen proteins to enter the cytoplasm
44
; or (2) direct fusion of the phagosome with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), delivering antigen proteins into the ER lumen, where they are further trimmed by ER aminopeptidases to a length of 8–11 amino acids. These peptides ultimately assemble with MHC-I molecules to form stable peptide-MHC-I complexes, which are then transported to the cell surface via the Golgi apparatus for recognition by CD8
+
T cells.
45
In this study, we designed ANM-NPs and ANM-NPs@T-Ag to enhance tumor antigen presentation and to modulate the tumor microenvironment, thereby triggering antitumor immune responses. ANM-NPs@T-Ag activates the complement pathway in mice and promotes DCs maturation, antigen internalization and presentation via mannose receptors and complement receptors. Experimental results demonstrated that, compared with traditional aluminum adjuvant-loaded whole-cell tumor antigen systems, ANM-NPs@T-Ag significantly enhanced the expression of MHC class molecules, CD80, and CD86 on the surface of DCs, indicating the potential of ANM-NPs as antigen adjuvants.
T cells undergo different differentiation states: the initial memory stem cell state (TSCM) has self-renewal and long-term survival potential, which is beneficial for sustained antitumor immune responses. Central memory T cells (TCM) and effector T cells exhibit strong proliferation and cytotoxicity but have shorter lifespans. Terminally differentiated effector T cells are highly cytotoxic but struggle to survive long-term in the tumor microenvironment.
46
Our findings showed that both intratumoral and subcutaneous administration of ANM-NPs@T-Ag resulted in significant antitumor effects. We first observed that ANM-NPs@T-Ag effectively suppressed tumor growth through intratumoral injection, enhancing the infiltration of DCs and T cells in the tumor microenvironment. Subcutaneous injection of ANM-NPs@T-Ag has the same effect. In the spleen, we detected a significant increase in TCM and TSCM, suggesting that ANM-NPs@T-Ag can activate the immune system, promote the generation and activation of antigen-specific T cells, and inhibit tumor growth. It also suggests ANM-NPs@T-Ag preserves the memory of tumor immunotherapy. Subcutaneous treatment with ANM-NPs@T-Ag induced a systemic antitumor immune response, leading to the accumulation of immune cells in secondary lymphoid organs such as the spleen and lymph nodes, further promoting the infiltration of CD4
+
and CD8
+
T cells into the tumor. This indicates that ANM-NPs@T-Ag may combat tumor growth and spread by activating a comprehensive immune response. TNF exerts antitumor effects by damaging tumor blood vessels and inducing tumor cell necrosis. TNF can activate CD8
+
T cells and NK cells, enhancing their cytotoxicity against immunogenic tumor cells.
47
IL-12 exhibits strong antitumor activity
48
by enhancing Th1/Tc1 responses and recruiting T cells to the tumor.
48 49
Analysis of bulk RNA-seq data revealed that treatment with ANM-NPs@T-Ag and non-heat-inactivated mouse serum significantly upregulated TNF and chemokines in mouse DCs; however, the transcription of certain interleukins (such as IL-12) was suppressed. We speculate that mannose receptors and complement receptors may promote the expression of TNF, chemokines, and some interleukins, while exerting different regulatory effects on cytokines like IL-12.
This study also demonstrated that the combination of ANM-NPs@T-Ag with PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint inhibitors has a synergistic effect, further inhibiting tumor growth. This suggests that combining ANM-NPs@T-Ag with immune checkpoint inhibitors may be a more effective therapeutic strategy, capable of overcoming the mechanisms of tumor immune tolerance and enhancing treatment efficacy.
In summary, unlike other methods that use inactivated bacteria directly as adjuvants, this study prepared carbon nanopolymers (ANM-NPs) as antigen adjuvants that target mannose receptors and lectin pathways, simulating the glycan structures on yeast surfaces. The whole-cell tumor antigens vaccine (ANM-NPs@T-Ag) can activate antigen endocytosis, promote antigen presentation, enhance immune infiltration, stimulate the production of specific antibodies, and effectively inhibit tumor growth.
